---
title: "Estimating prevalence"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center")
```

```{r setup}
library(MMSpower)
```

A national malaria programme wants to know how common a drug-resistance
marker (say, a validated *kelch13* mutation) is in one region. Earlier
reports suggest about 20% of infections carry it, and the programme wants to
estimate the prevalence to within ±5 percentage points, with 95% confidence.

Two functions do the work: `design_precision()` says how many samples to
collect, and `estimate_prevalence()` analyses them once they are in.

## Part 1: Designing the study

### How many samples, ignoring clustering?

Start with the simplest case: every sample is independent (as if drawn by
simple random sampling across the region) and the test is perfect.

```{r}
d0 <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05)
d0
```

So `r d0$n` samples are needed. This is the familiar
$z^2 p(1-p) / \text{MOE}^2$ formula, rounded up. Two things drive it: the
margin of error (halving it roughly quadruples the sample size) and the
expected prevalence (the sample size is largest at 50%). If the expected
prevalence is uncertain, using a value closer to 50% is the cautious choice.

### An imperfect test

Molecular assays are good but not perfect. Suppose the assay has
sensitivity 90% and specificity 95%: it misses some true positives, and
some negatives are wrongly called positive.

```{r}
d_test <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05,
                           sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)
d_test$n
```

The sample size rises from `r d0$n` to `r d_test$n`. The reason is that the
analysis will correct the measured prevalence back to the true scale (the
Rogan-Gladen correction), and this correction stretches the confidence
interval by a factor of $1 / (Se + Sp - 1)$. To keep the same margin of
error on the true scale, more samples are needed. Specificity matters more
than its size suggests: at low prevalence, false positives can make up a
large share of the positives.

### Clustering: samples come from sites

In practice samples are collected at a number of sites (health facilities,
villages), not drawn at random from the whole region. People at the same
site tend to be more alike than people at different sites, so each extra
sample from a site adds less information than a sample from a new site.
The intra-cluster correlation (ICC) measures how strong this is, and the
design effect $D_{eff} = 1 + (n_{per\,site} - 1)\,\text{ICC}$ says how much the
sample size has to grow. For this tutorial we assume an ICC of 0.05, and go
back to a perfect test to keep the numbers simple.

There are two ways to fix the design, depending on what is constrained in
the field.

**Fixing people per site.** If each site can realistically collect 20
samples, solve for the number of sites:

```{r}
d_per <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_per_site = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_per
```

The study needs `r d_per$n_sites` sites of `r d_per$n_per_site` people,
`r d_per$n` samples in total.

**Fixing the number of sites.** If the programme already has 20 sentinel
sites, solve for the number of people per site:

```{r}
d_sites <- design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = 20, icc = 0.05)
d_sites
```

Each of the `r d_sites$n_sites` sites now needs `r d_sites$n_per_site`
people, `r d_sites$n` samples in total.

In both cases `n_eff` is the unclustered answer from the first section: the
clustered design carries the same information as `r d_sites$n_eff`
independent samples. Fixing the sites at 20 needs more samples in total
than fixing 20 people per site, because the people per site go up, and so
does the design effect.

**Too few sites.** With the number of sites fixed, there is a limit. Each
site is worth at most $1 / \text{ICC}$ independent samples, however many
people are tested there, so a small number of sites can never reach the
target precision:

```{r, error = TRUE}
design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = 10, icc = 0.05)
```

The error reports the best margin of error that 10 sites can give. The
options are to add sites, accept a wider margin of error, or (if there is
evidence for it) assume a smaller ICC.

### More sites, fewer samples

The same precision can be reached with many different numbers of sites, and
spreading the samples over more sites reduces the total needed:

```{r}
sites <- c(15, 20, 30, 50, 100)
total <- sapply(sites, function(k)
  design_precision(prevalence = 0.2, moe = 0.05, n_sites = k, icc = 0.05)$n)
data.frame(sites, per_site = total / sites, total)
```

With 15 sites the study needs `r total[1]` samples; with 100 sites, only
`r total[5]`, close to the `r d0$n` an unclustered survey would need. Each
new site brings in fresh information, whereas each extra sample at a site
partly repeats what that site has already shown. So, where the budget and
logistics allow, aim for more sites with fewer people at each. Site visits
cost money too, and the [Costing a study](tutorial-cost.html) tutorial shows
how to find the cheapest design.

## Part 2: Analysing the data

Suppose the programme settles on 20 sites of about 30 people, and records
the number of samples carrying the marker (`x`) and the number tested (`n`)
at each site:

```{r}
x <- c(4, 9, 6, 2, 11, 7, 5, 8, 3, 6, 10, 4, 7, 5, 12, 6, 3, 8, 5, 7)
n <- c(30, 32, 28, 31, 30, 29, 33, 30, 27, 31, 30, 32, 29, 30, 31, 28, 30, 30, 32, 29)
```

### The estimate

By default the ICC is estimated from the spread of the site prevalences,
and an exact (Clopper-Pearson) interval is returned:

```{r}
est <- estimate_prevalence(x, n)
est
```

The estimated prevalence is `r round(100 * est$prevalence, 1)`%, with a 95%
interval from `r round(100 * est$ci_lower, 1)`% to
`r round(100 * est$ci_upper, 1)`%. `deff` is the design effect worked out
from the estimated ICC, and `n_eff` is the number of independent samples
the clustered data are worth. `df` is the number of sites minus one: the
ICC was estimated from `r length(n)` sites, and the interval is widened a
little to allow for the uncertainty in that estimate (see below).

### Choosing an interval method

Three interval methods are available. They give the same point estimate
but different intervals:

```{r}
cp <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, ci_method = "clopper-pearson")
c(cp$ci_lower, cp$ci_upper)

wald <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, ci_method = "wald")
c(wald$ci_lower, wald$ci_upper)

ac <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, ci_method = "agresti-coull")
c(ac$ci_lower, ac$ci_upper)
```

With this much data and a prevalence well away from 0 they are close. The
differences matter for small samples or a prevalence near 0 or 1. There the
Wald interval is too narrow, has zero width when no positives are seen, and
its limits can fall below 0 or above 1. `estimate_prevalence()` cuts such
limits back to 0 or 1, but that hides the problem rather than fixing it.
Clopper-Pearson, the default, is the cautious choice, and Agresti-Coull a
good compromise. `design_precision()` sizes a study with the simpler Wald
formula, so a Clopper-Pearson interval usually comes out a little wider
than the margin of error the study was designed for. See
`?estimate_prevalence` for the details.

### Supplied or estimated ICC?

The interval depends on the ICC, and estimating an ICC needs data from many
sites: with only a handful, the estimate is unreliable. `estimate_prevalence()`
allows for this by widening the interval according to the number of sites
the ICC was estimated from. With many sites this makes little difference,
but with a handful the interval becomes very wide. So with few sites it is
often better to supply a cautious value, for example from earlier surveys in
similar settings:

```{r}
est_icc <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, icc = 0.05)
c(est_icc$ci_lower, est_icc$ci_upper)
```

With `r length(n)` sites the estimate is usable: it gave an ICC of
`r round(est$icc, 3)` and an interval from
`r round(100 * est$ci_lower, 1)`% to `r round(100 * est$ci_upper, 1)`%,
while supplying 0.05 gives `r round(100 * est_icc$ci_lower, 1)`% to
`r round(100 * est_icc$ci_upper, 1)`%. The
[clustering concepts](concept-clustering.html) article shows how variable
ICC estimates are with few sites.

### An imperfect test at analysis

If the assay is imperfect, give its sensitivity and specificity, and the
estimate and interval are corrected to the true-prevalence scale:

```{r}
est_test <- estimate_prevalence(x, n, sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)
c(est_test$prevalence, est_test$ci_lower, est_test$ci_upper)
```

The corrected prevalence is lower than the measured one, because at this
prevalence false positives outnumber missed cases, and the interval is
wider. The sensitivity and specificity given here should be the same values
assumed when the study was designed: the design only delivers the planned
margin of error if the analysis makes the same correction.
